courseTitle: Infrastructure as Code with Terraform for DevOps

slots.practicalActivity: Write out, side by side, the imperative steps (raw az or aws CLI commands) versus the declarative description of creating the same single real resource (e.g. a resource group or an S3 bucket), then actually run the imperative version by hand once so the difference is felt before Terraform does it declaratively starting next chapter.
slots.deliverable: A short written imperative-vs-declarative comparison plus one real resource created by hand via raw CLI commands, to be recreated declaratively later in this course.

slots.practicalActivity: Research and write a one-paragraph comparison of Terraform against at least one alternative (CloudFormation, Bicep, or Pulumi) specifically on multi-cloud support, since Northbridge Retail runs both Azure and AWS, naming the one concrete capability gap that rules out a single-cloud-only tool for them.
slots.deliverable: A written comparison naming the specific multi-cloud capability gap that rules out a single-cloud-only IaC tool for a two-cloud shop.

slots.practicalActivity: Diagram Terraform's own architecture for a dual-cloud Northbridge configuration — the CLI, the azurerm and aws providers, the state file, and the plan/apply cycle — labeling where each piece actually runs (local machine vs. remote backend vs. the cloud's own API).
slots.deliverable: A labeled architecture diagram showing the Terraform CLI, two providers, state, and the cloud APIs each provider talks to.

slots.practicalActivity: Install Terraform locally and confirm with `terraform -v`, create a main.tf with a `required_providers` block pinning both azurerm and aws, and run a real `terraform init`, confirming both provider plugins actually download and lock successfully.
slots.deliverable: Real `terraform init` output showing both the azurerm and aws providers installed and recorded in `.terraform.lock.hcl`.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a `locals` block using all five HCL value types (string, number, bool, list, map) for real Northbridge values — environment, instance_count, is_production, allowed_regions, tags — then build a `resource_name_prefix` with `${ }` interpolation and confirm the evaluated result in `terraform console`.
slots.deliverable: A `locals` block exercising every HCL value type plus a `terraform console` session proving the interpolated string evaluates correctly.

slots.practicalActivity: Write and run a real first resource end to end — an azurerm_resource_group or aws_s3_bucket — through `terraform init`, `terraform plan`, and `terraform apply`, then `terraform destroy` it to confirm the full lifecycle actually works against a real cloud account.
slots.deliverable: A real cloud resource created and then destroyed, with the full init/plan/apply/destroy terminal output captured.

slots.practicalActivity: Refactor the previous slot's resource to take its name and location from `variable` blocks with types and defaults, add an `output` exposing the created resource's ID, then add a real `data` source (e.g. `azurerm_client_config` or `aws_caller_identity`) and reference it from the resource.
slots.deliverable: A configuration using variables, an output, and a real data source, with `terraform output` showing the correct exposed value.

slots.practicalActivity: Use at least three real built-in Terraform functions in the current configuration — e.g. `lower()` on a name, `cidrsubnet()` for a real network calculation, and `join()` to build a tag string from a list — verifying each one's result independently in `terraform console`.
slots.deliverable: A configuration using 3 distinct built-in functions, each one's correct output verified independently in `terraform console`.

slots.practicalActivity: Make a change `terraform plan` shows as an in-place update (e.g. a tag edit) and a separate change that forces a replace (e.g. renaming a resource), running `plan` before every `apply` without skipping it and explicitly reading the +/-/-/+ symbols before confirming either one.
slots.deliverable: Two captured `terraform plan` outputs — one in-place update, one forced replacement — each followed by its matching `apply`.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter review for Terraform Fundamentals: write one complete, from-scratch configuration for a real Azure or AWS resource using variables, a data source, a built-in function, and an output — and run it through a full plan/apply/destroy cycle without skipping the plan step at either end.
slots.deliverable: One complete .tf configuration combining variables, a data source, a function, and an output, successfully applied and then destroyed.

slots.practicalActivity: Run `terraform apply` once locally with the default local backend and open the resulting terraform.tfstate file directly in a text editor to see the real tracked resource attributes Terraform recorded, comparing them line by line against what the .tf file actually declared.
slots.deliverable: A viewed raw terraform.tfstate file with a short written note on at least 2 attributes it tracks that weren't explicitly set in the .tf file.

slots.practicalActivity: Provision a real Azure Storage Account + container (or S3 bucket) specifically to hold state, add a `backend "azurerm"` (or `"s3"`) block pointing at it, run `terraform init` to migrate, and confirm via the cloud CLI that the state blob/object now actually exists remotely; then, in a second terminal, try running `terraform apply` while the first is still mid-apply to watch the backend's lock get enforced.
slots.deliverable: A real remote backend configuration with cloud-side CLI confirmation that state now lives remotely, plus terminal proof of a second concurrent apply being blocked by state locking.

slots.practicalActivity: Manually create one real resource through the Azure or AWS console/CLI outside Terraform entirely, write a matching resource block, bring it under management with `terraform import`, and confirm `terraform plan` shows zero diff immediately afterward.
slots.deliverable: One real resource created outside Terraform, successfully imported, with a `terraform plan` showing zero diff right after import.

slots.practicalActivity: Use `terraform state list` and `terraform state show <resource>` to inspect what's tracked, then practice recovery for real: `terraform state rm` one resource without destroying it in the cloud and re-import it, or use `terraform state mv` to rename its address without recreating it.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output of `state list`/`state show`, plus a demonstrated `state rm`+re-import or `state mv` that leaves the real cloud resource untouched throughout.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter review for State: starting from a resource with purely local state, migrate it to a real remote backend, confirm locking works via a concurrent apply attempt, and finish with `terraform state list` against the now-remote state to confirm nothing was lost in the migration.
slots.deliverable: One resource's state migrated from local to a real remote backend, with before/after `terraform state list` output proving nothing was lost.

slots.practicalActivity: Extract an existing resource block (e.g. the storage account) into a real local child module under modules/, replace the root's direct resource block with a `module` block pointing at it via a relative source, call it twice (dev and staging), and confirm `terraform plan` shows two separately addressed module instances.
slots.deliverable: A working local module plus a `terraform plan` showing two independently addressed instances of it (e.g. module.storage_dev and module.storage_staging).

slots.practicalActivity: Add `variable` blocks to the previous module for every value that differs between its two callers (environment, replication_type), and add an `output` exposing the created resource's ID back to the root module, confirming with `terraform output` that it resolves correctly for both the dev and staging instances.
slots.deliverable: A module with declared variable inputs and an output, with `terraform output` showing the correct, distinct value for each of its two instances.

slots.practicalActivity: Find a real, popular module on the public Terraform Registry relevant to Northbridge (e.g. a VPC module for AWS, or a resource-group/vnet module for Azure), pin it to an exact version, call it with real inputs, and run `terraform init` confirming Terraform downloads it from the registry rather than a local path; then reorganize your own local module from the previous slots into the standard file layout (main.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf) and pin it too, this time with a Git `ref` tag instead of a bare relative path.
slots.deliverable: A module block sourcing a real public Terraform Registry module pinned to an exact version, plus the student's own local module restructured into main/variables/outputs.tf and re-sourced via a pinned Git ref.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the required_providers + provider "azurerm" block with the required empty features {}, authenticate with `az login` against a real free-tier Azure subscription, set subscription_id, and run `terraform init` confirming the azurerm provider initializes against that real subscription.
slots.deliverable: Real `az login` + `terraform init` output confirming the azurerm provider is initialized against an actual Azure subscription.

slots.practicalActivity: Declare a real azurerm_virtual_network, subnet, network security group, and azurerm_linux_virtual_machine (smallest free-tier-eligible size), apply it, confirm with the Azure CLI or portal that the VM is actually running inside that VNet, then destroy it.
slots.deliverable: A real Azure VM provisioned and confirmed running inside a Terraform-defined VNet, then destroyed with `terraform destroy`.

lessons.title: App Services, Storage & Key Vault on Azure

slots.practicalActivity: Provision a real azurerm_service_plan + azurerm_linux_web_app, an azurerm_storage_account, and an azurerm_key_vault holding one secret, then read that secret back via an azurerm_key_vault_secret data source and wire it into the web app's app_settings.
slots.deliverable: A real running Azure App Service whose app settings include a value read live from a real Key Vault secret via a data source, not hardcoded.

slots.practicalActivity: Write an azurerm_kubernetes_cluster resource for a small real AKS cluster, apply it, then run `az aks get-credentials` against the Terraform-created cluster and confirm `kubectl get nodes` works.
slots.deliverable: A real AKS cluster created entirely through Terraform, confirmed reachable with `kubectl get nodes` after `az aks get-credentials`.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter review for Azure: tear down everything built in this chapter in reverse dependency order with `terraform destroy`, confirming in the Azure CLI or portal that the VM, App Service, Key Vault, and AKS cluster are all actually gone, then rebuild just the resource group and storage account from a clean apply to prove the configuration is reproducible.
slots.deliverable: Terminal proof of a full `terraform destroy` removing every Azure resource from this chapter, followed by a clean re-apply proving reproducibility.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the required_providers + provider "aws" block, configure a named AWS CLI profile with `aws configure --profile northbridge-prod` against a real free-tier AWS account, reference it via `profile`, and run `terraform init` confirming the aws provider authenticates with no hardcoded keys anywhere.
slots.deliverable: Real `aws configure --profile` setup plus `terraform init`/`terraform plan` output confirming the aws provider authenticates via a named profile with no hardcoded keys.

slots.practicalActivity: Declare a real aws_vpc, subnet, security group, and aws_instance (free-tier-eligible type), apply it, confirm with the AWS CLI or console that it's running inside the VPC you defined, then destroy it.
slots.deliverable: A real EC2 instance provisioned inside a Terraform-defined VPC, confirmed running, then destroyed.

slots.practicalActivity: Provision a real aws_s3_bucket, an aws_iam_role + policy granting a Lambda function access to just that bucket, and an aws_lambda_function with a small real deployment package, then invoke it with `aws lambda invoke` and confirm it reads/writes the bucket using only the IAM role, no hardcoded keys.
slots.deliverable: A real Lambda function, invoked successfully, reading or writing a real S3 bucket using only its Terraform-created IAM role.

slots.practicalActivity: Write an aws_eks_cluster resource (with its required IAM role and VPC/subnets) for a small real EKS cluster, apply it, then run `aws eks update-kubeconfig` against it and confirm `kubectl get nodes` works.
slots.deliverable: A real EKS cluster created entirely through Terraform, confirmed reachable with `kubectl get nodes` after `aws eks update-kubeconfig`.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter review for AWS: tear down everything built in this chapter in reverse dependency order with `terraform destroy`, confirming in the AWS console or CLI that the EC2 instance, Lambda function, S3 bucket, and EKS cluster are all gone, then write a short note comparing the AWS destroy order against the Azure chapter's to show you understand why dependency order matters for destroy, not just apply.
slots.deliverable: Terminal proof of a full `terraform destroy` removing every AWS resource from this chapter, plus a short written comparison of destroy-order dependencies versus Azure.

slots.practicalActivity: Create real `dev` and `staging` Terraform workspaces for one resource named with `terraform.workspace` interpolated in, apply in each and confirm two separate resources exist; then write a real GitHub Actions workflow running `terraform fmt -check`, `terraform plan`, and (on merge to main) `terraform apply` using OIDC/workload-identity auth instead of a stored secret.
slots.deliverable: Two real resources created via separate Terraform workspaces, plus a working GitHub Actions workflow file running fmt/plan/apply with OIDC auth and no stored cloud secret.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real policy check (OPA/Conftest, Sentinel, or a tfsec/checkov static scan) that rejects a resource missing a required tag, proving it blocks a noncompliant plan and passes a compliant one; separately, manually change a real deployed resource's setting directly in the cloud console and confirm `terraform plan` correctly detects and reports the drift.
slots.deliverable: A policy check blocking one noncompliant configuration and passing a compliant one, plus a `terraform plan` output correctly detecting a real, manually-introduced drift.

slots.practicalActivity: Take a resource from an earlier chapter and replace any hardcoded secret with a live `data` source read from Azure Key Vault or AWS Secrets Manager, confirm the secret never appears in the .tf file or in `git diff`, and add a real .gitignore excluding *.tfvars, *.tfstate*, and .terraform/.
slots.deliverable: A configuration reading a real secret live via a data source (not hardcoded), a correct .gitignore, and `git status` confirming state/tfvars files are untracked.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: Provision a Production-Style Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Write the capstone's scope document for a production-style, dual-cloud Northbridge Retail environment: list every Azure and AWS resource type it will include (networking, compute/App Service, storage, a managed Kubernetes cluster, IAM/Key Vault secrets) and the remote-backend and module structure it must use.
slots.deliverable: A written capstone scope/requirements document naming every Azure and AWS resource type to be provisioned and the backend/module structure to be used.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the capstone exactly as scoped: a root configuration calling shared azure-network and aws-network modules side by side, provider-specific resources (App Service, S3, Lambda) tagged consistently from one local.common_tags map, all against a real remote backend, running a real `terraform plan` to confirm the full multi-cloud resource set before applying it.
slots.deliverable: A real `terraform plan` showing the correct full set of Azure and AWS resources about to be created across two modules, followed by a successful `terraform apply` against a real remote backend.

slots.practicalActivity: Run `terraform destroy` to tear down the whole capstone environment cleanly, confirm in both cloud consoles that nothing billable remains, then record a short screen-captured walkthrough (or write a structured portfolio writeup) of the terraform plan/apply output and the module/backend architecture, framed as a portfolio piece for a job interview.
slots.deliverable: A confirmed clean `terraform destroy` across both clouds, plus a portfolio artifact (recorded demo or written walkthrough with real terminal output) explaining the capstone's architecture for a job interview.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can write real, production-habited Terraform configurations — variables, data sources, modules, and remote state with locking — that provision actual networking, compute, storage, managed Kubernetes clusters, and secrets on both Azure and AWS, run safely through CI/CD, and tear down cleanly on demand.
